explainers.title: Getting started: our active chant
explainers.body: Look at a picture of children playing, or go outside and watch a game. What can you see? What are the children doing? Then read this chant out loud together. Clap along, and join in on the last line!

explainers.title: 1. What keeps us healthy?
explainers.body:
Three things help us stay healthy and strong. We move and play. We eat good food. We sleep well. Read each one with your grown-up. Tick the healthy things you did today.

Healthy food helps our bodies grow strong. Near us we have good foods like banana, mango, camel milk and beans. What healthy food do you like best?
bullets: ☐ I ran, played, or moved my body.
☐ I ate some healthy food, like fruit, milk or beans.
☐ I drank some water.
☐ I had a good sleep last night.

explainers.title: 2. How does it feel when we are active?
explainers.body:
When we are active, our body changes. Our heart beats fast. We breathe big breaths. We feel warm. Our feelings change too. We can feel happy, excited and proud. Read these two diaries with your grown-up. Then find the feeling words.

Layla wrote: On Saturday I played football at the maidan. I felt excited when I ran fast. I scored a goal, and I felt so happy and proud. At the end I was tired, but it was fun.

Omar wrote: We had a running race at school. I did not win. At first I felt a little disappointed. But I tried my best, and my team cheered for me. That made me feel proud.

headers: My most active day (draw it here)

explainers.title: 3. A healthy day
explainers.body:
We can be active and healthy all day long. Draw or write one healthy thing for each part of the day. Two are done to help you start.

Here are three big activity words. Can you show each one with your body? Run on the spot for endurance. Make strong arms for strength. Touch your toes for flexibility!

rows: keep going for a long time

explainers.title: 4. Ways to be active near me
explainers.body:
There are lots of ways to be active where we live. You do not need a special place. You can run, skip or play in a yard, a maidan, or a park. Tick the ones you like. Add your own idea at the end.

The place near where you live is your area. Now say which activity you would like to try. Use these words: I would like to try ... and I want to ...
bullets: ☐ play football (kubbadda cagta)
☐ run or have a race
☐ skip with a rope
☐ play a running-and-catching game
☐ go for a walk with my family

explainers.title: 5. Reading a map with Bilal
explainers.body:
My friend Bilal loves maps. A map is a picture of a place from above, like a bird sees it. It shows where the places are. A compass helps us say the way: North is up, South is down, and East and West are the sides.

Here are the places on Bilal's map of his part of Hargeisa. Circle the places that are good for being active. Look for the big open spaces with no buildings.

headers: My map (draw your home and a place to be active)

explainers.title: 6. A little survey
explainers.body:
A survey means asking lots of people the same question. Then we count the answers. First, let's read what one class found out. They asked their friends: Have you ever been to these places?

Look at the numbers. Are these true or false? Say the answer with your grown-up.

A fact is something true you can check. An opinion is what someone thinks. Read these. Which is a fact? Which is an opinion?

Now do your own little survey. Choose three places near you. Ask a few children: Have you ever been to ...? Make a tally mark for each yes.

Ask them what they think, too: What was your opinion of ...? Top tip: before you ask, think about how you will show your answers.
bullets: More than 10 children have been to the maidan.
Exactly 10 children have been to the park.
Fewer than 10 children have been to the community centre.

rows: 16 children have been to the maidan.
The maidan is the best place to play.
You can run at the park.
The park is more fun than the maidan.

explainers.title: 7. An activity I would like to try
explainers.body:
Now choose one activity you would like to try, or get better at. It could be football, skipping, running, or something else. How can you find out more about it? There are three ways. Tick the ones you could try.

An expert is a person who knows a lot about something. Maybe an expert can visit, like Coach Faadumo, who teaches football at the maidan. What would you ask her? Here are some good questions:

Listen carefully to the answers. Try to remember the important words.
bullets: ☐ Ask someone who knows, like a coach or an older cousin.
☐ Read a book about it.
☐ Look online with a grown-up.
Where can I do it?
What do I need to bring?
Do I need special shoes or clothes?
An activity I would like to try is ...
A place where I could do it is ...
I would still like to know about ...

explainers.title: 8. Start planning our stall
explainers.body:
Soon your group will make a stall with a leaflet about a healthy activity or a place to be active. Start to think about it now. What will your group choose? Sagal's group chose football at the maidan.

Tell your group your idea. Listen to their ideas too. You will make the stall together on the next sheet!

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You found out so much about being active and healthy today! Answer these out loud with your grown-up.

Well done! Now turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to make your very own stall and leaflet.
bullets: What is one thing you like to do to be active?
Where is a good place near you to be active?
How does being active make you feel?

At another stall, Omar's group showed everyone skipping (boodbood), a game children have played for a long, long time. They persuaded a friend to try it. They said where you can play, why it is good for you, and the skills you need. They answered good questions, like 'Can you use any rope?' and 'What are the rules?'
Now think of two good questions you could ask at another stall. Write or draw them here.

lines: We will listen to everyone's ideas.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.
notes: please read every part aloud. Your child can point, talk, draw, tick and colour. Some parts are best done outside, moving your bodies. There are no marks. Just have fun together.

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to your child's Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up who will run the unit with your child. Six- and seven-year-olds are early readers, so you will read most of it aloud, look at the pictures together, and do lots of talking. Underneath all that fun, your child is quietly growing big skills: finding things out, reading a simple map, sorting what is true from what is a thought, saying what they think, showing and telling, working with others, and looking back at their learning.

This project grows those skills through a topic every child loves: being active. Children of this age love to run, jump, kick and play. So this is the perfect place to grow their thinking. Together you will explore how being active keeps us healthy and happy, where we can go to play near us, and how to tell other people all about it.

You do not need to be a teacher, and you do not need anything special. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, some paper and crayons, and a bit of space to move, such as a yard, a maidan (an open field), or a room with the chairs pushed back. That is how these skills grow.

sections.title: About this project: How can we be active and healthy?
sections.body:
Over this unit, you and your child will explore one big, happy question: how can we be active and healthy? Your child will find out how being active makes our body and our feelings feel, discover good places to be active near us, find out about an activity they would like to try, and hear what other children think. Then, best of all, your child's group will make a stall with a leaflet about a healthy activity or a place to be active, and tell everyone about it.

The journey is broken into six short, picture-led lessons (3.1 to 3.6), then the group stall and leaflet, then a gentle looking-back. The topic is the fun part; the real learning is happening quietly underneath it.

sections.title: The skills your child will gently grow
sections.body:
This project grows several Global Perspectives skills. Here they are in plain words, with what to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give any marks. You simply give your child lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A warm 'That was great finding out, Sagal' teaches more than any worksheet.
items: Finding out (research) — asking, looking, reading, and looking online with you, to learn about an activity or a place. Listen for: 'Where can I do that?'
Reading a map and sorting (a little analysis) — reading a simple map, and telling a fact from an opinion. Listen for: 'That one is true, but that one is just what she thinks.'
Saying what I think (opinion) — telling which activity they would like to try, and why. Listen for: 'I would like to try ... because ...'
Showing and telling (communication) — making a clear leaflet and telling others about it, and asking good questions. Listen for: 'Come and see our stall!'
Working together (collaboration) — sharing the jobs in a group, taking turns, and helping each other make the stall.
Thinking about our learning (reflection) — looking back at what they know now, and what helped them learn.

sections.title: The learning goals, in child-friendly words
sections.body: Here are the little goals for this unit. They are written the way we say them to children. There are no codes to remember.
items: I can talk about what people do to be active, and how it feels.
I can talk about activities I could try.
I can find out about places to be active near me.
I can find out what other children like to do.
I can find out about an activity I would like to try.
I can say what I think, and why.
I can help my group make a leaflet and a stall about a healthy activity.
I can tell other children about our stall, and ask and answer questions.
I can talk about what I learned, and what helped me.

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age are still early readers, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's young model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no fixed timetable. Spread the six lessons across two or three weeks, or longer. If your child wants to run around the maidan five times, wonderful. Curiosity and joy are the whole point.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read the pages and the active chant aloud, run the simple activities, and keep it all warm and playful. Each lesson is short, about 20 to 30 minutes, and you can split it into smaller pieces. Some parts are best done outside, moving your bodies.
Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these live sessions, children share their maps and their stalls, and hear other children too. The group stall works best with a few children together.

A 24-hour AI tutor, always used with a grown-up. The tutor can read a page aloud, ask your child a friendly question, help look up an activity, or be a pretend visitor while your child practises the stall. At this age the tutor is always used with you beside your child, never alone.

sections.title: Meet Sagal and her friends
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a little girl called Sagal. She goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa, and she loves to run, skip and play football. Your child can imagine being active right alongside her and her friends.

They also meet a helper called Coach Faadumo, a woman who teaches football to girls and boys at the maidan. She is an expert — someone who knows a lot about an activity. Together the children are a little team. As your child meets each new idea, they will see what Sagal's team does with it. Later, your child will do the very same thing with their own team, which can be classmates, brothers and sisters, or friends.
items: Sagal loves to move and play. She runs fast, she loves football, and she is kind and good at listening.
Bilal likes maps and finding places. He is good at pointing the way.
Hodan loves to find out how things work and asks lots of questions.
Ayaan has lots of ideas and loves to draw pictures.
Layla likes talking to people and asking them questions.
Omar likes to help and to share the jobs fairly. He is good at showing others how to warm up.

sections.title: How to read the picture pages and the active chant aloud
sections.body:
Each lesson begins with a picture and lots of talking. The unit opens with a busy picture of a sports and activity day, full of children trying things out. The Activity Sheet also has a short active chant to enjoy together. Here is how to make the most of them:

The chant carries the unit's big message: sport is fun, and it is for everyone. Make sure girls hear loud and clear that football, running and every game are for them too.
items: Look first. Point to things in the sports-day picture and name them together: children running, a ball, a skipping rope, a coach, a stall, leaflets.
Ask gentle questions. 'Where are the children? What is each one doing? Have you ever tried that? What do you like to play?'
Read the chant slowly, with a beat. Clap along as you read. Let your child join in on the last line, then read it again faster for a giggle.
Say the words warmly. Enjoy the sounds of the activities: football (kubbadda cagta), running, skipping, jumping, and playing at the maidan.
Let your child talk more than you. A picture is a doorway to talking. Follow where your child leads.

sections.title: How to run the six short lessons
sections.body: Each lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for, just for you), a Talk about part (to get your child thinking and speaking), and a Do part (the hands-on activity). Read the Aim to yourself, then enjoy the Talk about and Do parts together. Lots of talking, and lots of moving, is exactly right.

sections.title: Lesson 3.1 - How do we feel when we are active?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child learns that being active keeps us healthy, and that it changes how our body and our feelings feel.

Talk about. Ask: 'What do you like to do to move and play? How do you feel after you run and play?' Let your child jump up and show you.

Do. Talk about three things that keep us healthy: being active, eating healthy food, and sleeping well. Then be active together for a minute (run on the spot, jump, or dance) and notice what changes: a fast heart, warm skin, big breaths, and a happy feeling. Remind your child that you do not always need a special place. Read the two little diaries in the Activity Sheet and find the feeling words together, then make a healthy-day timetable.

sections.title: Lesson 3.2 - Where can we go to be active?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child finds out about places to be active near us, using a simple map, and finds out what other children like by doing a little survey.

Talk about. Ask: 'Where do children go to run and play near us? Is there a maidan, a park, or an open field?'

Do. Look at a simple map together (there is one to read and one to draw in the Activity Sheet). Show the compass: North is up, South is down, East and West are the sides. Circle the places that are good for being active — the ones with big open spaces and no buildings. Then do a little survey: ask a few children 'Have you ever been to the maidan?' and keep count with tally marks. Talk about the difference between a fact (16 children have been to the maidan) and an opinion (the maidan is the best place).

sections.title: Lesson 3.3 - What activity would we like to try?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child chooses an activity to find out more about, thinks of good questions for an expert, and says what they think.

Talk about. Ask: 'Is there an activity you would like to try, or get better at? How could we find out more about it?'

Do. With the group, list activities children can do in your area, and choose one to find out more about. Talk about three ways to find out: ask people, read a book, or look online with you. If you can, invite an expert to visit — a local coach, a PE teacher, or an older cousin who is good at the activity. Help your child think of relevant questions (Where can I do it? What do I need to bring? Do I need special shoes?) and listen for the key words in the answer. Finish with the opinion frame: 'An activity I would like to try is ...; a place where I could do it is ...; I would still like to know about ...'.

sections.title: Lesson 3.4 - Making our stall and leaflet together
sections.body:
Aim. Your child and their group choose a healthy activity or place, and begin to make a leaflet and a stall about it.

Talk about. Ask: 'What healthy activity or place should we tell people about? Why is it good?'

Do. Help the group choose Option 1 (an activity, like football or skipping) or Option 2 (a place, like the maidan or the park). Choose the messages for the leaflet (it is fun / it makes you healthy / it is easy to do here / it is for everyone / it is for people who like a challenge / it helps you make friends). Plan the leaflet with the checklist: the activity, where you can do it, why you should do it, and pictures. Then decide what else to show on the stall — objects, pictures, and one skill to demonstrate, like how to warm up or how to kick safely. The full steps are in the Mini-Project sheet.

sections.title: Lesson 3.5 - Telling others about our stall
sections.body:
Aim. Your child tells others about the stall, persuades them kindly to try the activity, and asks and answers good questions, including a follow-up question.

Talk about. Ask: 'What will you say to make someone want to try our activity? What good questions could you ask at another stall?'

Do. Help the group practise. First rehearse at home with you and, if you like, the AI tutor as a pretend visitor. Then present for real to the family or to other children in the teacher session. Show your child how to persuade kindly by saying why the activity is fun, healthy and for everyone. Practise asking relevant questions (What are the rules? Where can I play?) rather than unhelpful ones (Who is the best player in the world?). Then teach the follow-up question: a second question to find out more (for example, 'Is there a football club near us?' then 'Can children our age join?'). At the end, let your child choose a favourite stall and say why.

sections.title: Lesson 3.6 - What have we learned?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child looks back at the whole project and thinks about their learning and their teamwork.

Talk about. Ask: 'What do you know now about being active and healthy that you did not know before? What helped you learn?'

Do. Use the reflection in the Mini-Project sheet. Your child talks about what they know and can do now, a good idea a friend had, how the group helped each other, and what helped them learn (such as a map with a key). Keep it warm and spoken. This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill, and it matters as much as the stall.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the words your child will meet in this project. Say them often and warmly. There is no need to test them.

rows: Strong and well in your body.
Moving your body a lot, like running, jumping or playing.
Moving your body to keep it strong, like sport or play.
Moving your body to make it strong and well.
Being able to keep going for a long time.
Being bendy, so you can reach, bend and stretch.
The place near where you live.
A picture that shows where places are, seen from above.
A helper that shows the way: North, South, East and West.
A big empty space with no buildings, good for playing.
Asking lots of people the same question to find out what they think.
A little line you make to count each answer.
Something true that you can check.
What a person thinks. Other people may think something different.
A person who knows a lot about something.
A little paper with words and pictures that tells people about something.
A little table where you show your work to visitors.
To help someone want to do something.
A second question you ask to find out more.
To stand up and tell others about your work.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy. Gather a few of these before you start, and keep them in a box:
items: Paper and crayons or coloured pencils.
A ball, a skipping rope, or anything to play with outside (nice, but not needed).
One big sheet of paper for the group leaflet, and a small table for the stall.
A simple map of your neighbourhood, or just draw one (there is a space in the Activity Sheet).
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.
A little space to move: a yard, a maidan, a park, or a room with the chairs pushed back.
A warm voice and a little time, about twice a week.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient, friendly helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in your child's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep it short and cheerful, and always stay in the room. The tutor helps your child get ready; then the real, proud moment is presenting the stall to family or friends in the teacher session. If the tutor ever suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it. You are always in charge.
items: Read aloud. Ask it to read a page, the active chant, or a checklist slowly, so your child can follow.
Ask a friendly question. Ask it to ask your child one question about being active, then let your child answer out loud to you.
Help find out. Ask it about an activity your child wants to try, or where you might play it near you, then talk about the answer together.
Help practise the stall. Let the tutor be a friendly pretend visitor while your child rehearses what to say at the stall.

sections.title: The final task: a stall with a leaflet
sections.body: Everything leads to this. In a small team, your child will choose a healthy activity or a place to be active, make a leaflet about it, set up a stall, and then present it to others and answer their questions. The full, child-friendly steps are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Your role is to gather the bits and pieces, keep the team kind and fair, and help only when they are truly stuck. A bright, hand-made leaflet that the children are proud of is a complete success.

sections.title: Simple ways to support and extend
sections.body:
Every child is different. Here are gentle ways to make the unit easier, or to add a little more for a child who is ready.

To support a child who finds it tricky:

To extend a child who wants more:
items: Read every part aloud, and let your child point, draw, or act it out instead of writing.
Do the activity outside first — run, skip or kick a ball — then talk about how it felt.
Do one small piece at a time, and stop while it is still fun.
Let your child talk their answer instead of writing it. Talking always counts.
Try the Daily Mile: run or walk around the maidan each day and count the days.
Draw a bigger map with more places, and add a compass with North, South, East and West.
Find out about one new activity, and teach you three facts about it.
Let your child be the expert and answer your questions about their favourite activity.

sections.title: Keeping it warm and fun
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, celebrate every jump and every drawing, and talk far more than you worry about getting it 'right'. If your child finishes this unit knowing that being active makes us healthy and happy, that there are good places to play near us, and that sport is for everyone, then this project has done its job beautifully. Have fun, and be active, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is the big one! At Ehel Academy, Sagal and her friends made a stall with a leaflet about a healthy activity, and now it is your turn. With your group and a grown-up, you will make a leaflet and a stall to tell people about a healthy activity or a place to be active. Then you will look back and think about how your team did. Take your time, share the jobs, and be kind to each other.

steps.title: Choose your activity or place
steps.intro:
Talk together and choose one thing to tell people about. You can choose an activity or a place.

Sagal's group chose football at the maidan. It is fun, it is healthy, and it is for everyone — girls and boys. Write or draw your choice here.
items: Option 1 — an activity: football (kubbadda cagta), skipping, running, or a running-and-catching game.

steps.title: Practise, then present
steps.intro:
Before you show your stall to everyone, practise first. Rehearse at home with your grown-up, and with your AI tutor as a pretend visitor. Then present for real to your family, or to other children in the teacher session.

When you present, try to persuade people to try your activity. Persuade means helping someone want to do it. Use this checklist. Tick each one when you have said it.

steps.title: Ask and answer good questions
steps.intro:
At the stalls, you will ask questions and answer questions. A good question is a relevant one — it helps you find out about the activity. Read these questions. Draw a happy face next to the good questions. Draw a straight face next to the ones that do not help much.

When you have seen all the stalls, choose your favourite. Colour some stars for it. Then say why you liked it. Finish these: My favourite stall was ... and I liked it because ...
